lesson.title: One Gene, Many Proteins: The Logic of Alternative Splicing
lesson.summary: By including or skipping different exons from the same pre-mRNA, a cell can generate several distinct mature mRNAs, and therefore several distinct protein variants, from a single gene.
lesson.body:
Splicing does not have to happen the same way every time a given pre-mRNA is processed. Because a gene's coding information is already broken into discrete exon blocks separated by removable introns, a cell has room to decide, transcript by transcript, which exons to keep. An exon that is included in one version of the mature mRNA can be skipped entirely in another, a nearby intron can occasionally be retained instead of removed, or a splice site can be shifted slightly to lengthen or shorten a neighboring exon. Each of these outcomes, generated from identical starting pre-mRNA using the same spliceosome machinery described earlier, produces a different final mRNA sequence, and therefore a different protein.

This matters enormously for how much protein diversity a genome can support. The human genome contains roughly twenty thousand protein-coding genes, a modest number for an organism as complex as a human being, yet human cells collectively produce a much larger set of distinct proteins. Alternative splicing is one of the main reasons that gap exists: a single gene can act as a template for multiple related but functionally distinct proteins, expressed in different tissues or at different times, without the genome needing a separate gene for each variant.

A classic example is the tropomyosin gene, which is spliced differently in different cell types. Skeletal muscle cells, smooth muscle cells, and non-muscle cells such as fibroblasts each splice the tropomyosin pre-mRNA to include a different combination of exons, producing tropomyosin proteins with different properties suited to each cell's specific structural needs, all from one starting gene. Whatever combination of exons ends up in the final mRNA, that transcript still needs its 5' cap and poly-A tail to be stable and exportable, and it still needs an intact reading frame running from a start codon to a stop codon, which is why alternative splicing has to be a highly regulated process rather than a haphazard one.
